entities.summary:
Filippo Calendario (died 1355) was a master architect and sculptor from Venice, whose pivotal role in the design and initial construction of the iconic Doge's Palace during the 14th century firmly established his place in Venetian architectural history. His work, blending Gothic and Byzantine influences, became a defining element of the city's unique aesthetic and political grandeur, symbolizing the maritime republic's growing power and wealth. Calendario's career, however, ended abruptly and dramatically with his execution for treason, a testament to the turbulent political climate of the Venetian Republic.

Calendario's primary known contribution was his involvement in the reconstruction of the Doge's Palace following a devastating fire in 1340. Historical records, particularly the 'Mariegola dei Tagliapietra' (Statutes of the Stonecutters), attribute to him the design and supervision of the palace's southern facade overlooking the Riva degli Schiavoni, including the famous portico and the initial phase of the Sala del Maggior Consiglio (Great Council Hall). This monumental undertaking, initiated around 1341, transformed the existing Byzantine-era fortress into a more elaborate Gothic governmental seat, reflecting the Republic's ambition. He employed innovative structural techniques for the weighty upper floors, utilizing arcades and loggias that appeared delicate yet supported massive stone walls.
